name: Progressivism
summary: Progressivism seeks deliberate social improvement through democratic reform, wider effective freedom and a fairer distribution of opportunity and economic resources. Its defining accounts support public action to counter concentrated power while differing over institutional design, ownership and the role of religion. Contemporary self-definitions also emphasise sustainability and cooperation.
scope: The political reform tradition described by Thompson (s28), CAP’s defining intellectual and human-rights studies (s17, s16), the Encyclopedia of Religion and Society (s9), and Compass’s account of progressive politics (s27). These sources discuss historical American progressivism and its later development, alongside a British definition combining democracy, equality and sustainability; the name is not reduced to a present-day US caucus. Croly’s The Promise of American Life and Dewey’s The Public and Its Problems count only as the specific seminal/canonical works that s17 identifies. An organisation’s account of progressive principles is used as a definition, not as authority for its wider platform. Historical exclusions and religious contributions are not removed by definition; a general observation that the movement varies does not itself answer a statement.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: In Chapter X Croly says a peace-seeking democracy must be physically prepared to fight and advocates sufficient naval strength to sustain its foreign commitments.

abolish-income-tax.rationale: Thompson identifies income taxation as an explicit progressive means of paying for social provision and reducing unequal wealth.

abortion-legal.rationale: Shalin describes the defence of women’s reproductive rights against restrictive state laws and court decisions as part of contemporary progressive politics.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: The human-rights study identifies the UDHR as a statement of progressive values; Article 18 explicitly protects changing one’s religion or belief.

ban-cartels.rationale: Thompson distinguishes trust-busting progressives from the New Nationalist approach of regulating large combinations instead of breaking them up.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Shalin describes progressive reform as an effort to salvage capitalism through reconstruction instead of overthrowing it.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: The intellectual history describes progressivism as retaining the gains of technology, industrialisation and capitalism while countering corporate power and unequal opportunity.

central-planning.rationale: Shalin defines the reformers’ project as reconstructing capitalism rather than adopting a command economy or massive nationalisation.

change-traditions-that-no-longer-suit.rationale: The intellectual history describes laws and institutions as revisable when changed social conditions make inherited arrangements unable to serve freedom and democracy.

character-from-environment.rationale: Dewey’s Chapter V describes effective intelligence and social habits as developed through education, culture and institutions rather than fixed faculties present in isolation.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: The intellectual history assigns government an organised responsibility for protecting people from insecurity; Croly’s Chapter XII rejects leaving wealth’s public duties to accidental private benevolence.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Croly’s Chapter VIII explicitly defends temporary colonial tutelage of Asian and African societies, while Compass’s definition criticises the colonial hierarchy of civilised societies ruling others as regressive.

collective-bargaining.rationale: Croly’s Chapter XII would set minimum wages and working hours through bargaining between employer organisations and unions while permitting additional individual rewards above the minimum.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Thompson places government by the people at the centre of progressive political philosophy and explains reforms intended to make that authority effective.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Shalin describes contemporary progressivism as trying to correct the exclusion of racial minorities from earlier reforms and to address the legacy of segregation and discrimination.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: In Chapter VII Croly defends an independent judiciary’s duty to interpret the Constitution, while calling for a more amendable constitution rather than judicial subordination to passing majorities.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: The human-rights study describes progressive social provision of food, housing, education and health care as indispensable to the effective exercise of political freedom.

democracy-best.rationale: Thompson describes democracy as the core of progressive political philosophy, defended both as morally legitimate and as more reliable over time than rule by a few.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: Croly’s Chapter VII says popular sovereignty can produce anti-democratic government; Dewey’s Chapter V likewise distinguishes democratic social life from its electoral machinery.

direct-votes.rationale: Thompson identifies initiative and referendum as progressive means of letting voters directly make or repeal laws.

distribution-by-process.rationale: Thompson identifies a more equitable distribution of wealth as a defining progressive aim and rejects treating existing fortunes as proof of personal virtue alone.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: The human-rights study accepts limited, temporary derogations from some ordinary rights during genuine public emergencies while preserving nonderogable protections.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: The human-rights study argues that international human-rights commitments need legitimate avenues of redress and actual enforcement powers against abusive states.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Shalin describes progressive reformers’ commitment to retaining constitutional safeguards against one-party tyranny, while reconstructing economic and democratic institutions.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The human-rights study explicitly presents equal human dignity and rights as core progressive values, grounded in common humanity.

every-country-ready-for-democracy.rationale: Croly’s Chapter VIII explicitly claims that most Asian and African societies were not then capable of national democratic government and uses that claim to defend tutelage.

family-wage.rationale: The human-rights study treats the UDHR as a statement of progressive values; Article 23 in its appendix requires remuneration sufficient for a worker and family to live in dignity.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Thompson describes progressive income taxation as part of using public power to reduce wealth inequalities; Shalin expressly includes progressive income tax and inheritance surcharges among reform tenets.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: In Chapter IV Croly calls the Union’s military prevention of Southern secession justifiable coercion and rejects accepting peaceful disunion as the better course.

gradual-change.rationale: Croly’s Chapter IX rejects suddenly uprooting essential national institutions and requires demonstrated need, discussion and public consent for substantial changes.

indirect-election.rationale: Thompson identifies direct popular election of senators, replacing election by state legislatures, as a central progressive reform.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Thompson says progressive writers welcomed industrial and technological possibilities and sought a fairer distribution of their benefits rather than abandoning industrial society.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: The human-rights study grounds progressive rights in the UDHR; Article 16 in its appendix explicitly rejects religious limitations on marriage.

international-criminal-courts.rationale: The human-rights study supports international accountability for crimes against humanity and describes the ICC as a mechanism to prosecute when national authorities cannot or will not act.

limit-growth.rationale: Compass’s defining account connects the costs of unchecked economic progress with the climate crisis and presents degrowth and redistribution as a potentially more progressive approach than growth-first policy.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Thompson defines progressivism by its rejection of laissez-faire and its demand for public control of economic activity to reduce inequality.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Dewey’s Chapter V explicitly rejects an economic determinism that overlooks how knowledge, communication and shared meanings change the consequences of industrial forces.

means-match-ends.rationale: Compass explicitly says that means shape ends and uses this principle to judge which kinds of change deserve to be called progressive.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Compass’s definition rejects a politics of hostility toward outsiders and treats respect for individuals and collaboration across groups as requirements of progressive politics.

minority-veto.rationale: Dewey’s Chapter VI defends majority decision after discussion, persuasion and a fair chance for minorities to become majorities; it does not give each dissenting group a veto.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: Croly’s Chapter XII favours public ownership combined with private operation of municipal utilities, while distinguishing those responsibilities from direct public administration.

more-religion-public.rationale: The faith study calls for religious voices to renew progressive public discourse and moral action while retaining a role for the secular tradition.

municipal-businesses-mixed-economy.rationale: Thompson identifies municipal ownership of public utilities among progressive economic reforms within a wider system retaining private enterprise.

nation-first.rationale: The human-rights study rejects advancing national security without regard to legitimate means and favours international human-rights law and global political cooperation.

night-watchman-state.rationale: CAP’s defining account assigns government responsibility for business regulation, economic opportunity and social protection beyond defence, policing and property.

no-business-privileges.rationale: Thompson describes the progressive challenge to vested economic interests and to financial domination of government, aimed at replacing privileged influence with public control.

one-party-rule.rationale: Shalin describes the progressive rejection of the Bolshevik one-party state and insistence on constitutional safeguards and democratic reform.

participatory-democracy.rationale: The intellectual history identifies greater democratic control over workplaces, homes, neighbourhoods and the environment as practical implications of progressive philosophy.

party-controls-media.rationale: In Chapter V Dewey requires free social inquiry and dissemination of its results and criticises censorship and control of opinion as obstacles to democratic public judgment.

patriotism-serves-workers.rationale: The intellectual history describes a national democratic community whose public power should protect workers and families from concentrated economic power.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: The intellectual history describes corporate domination of public institutions and a corrupt political class as problems progressivism seeks to overcome.

positive-liberty.rationale: The intellectual history explicitly distinguishes effective freedom to pursue chosen ends from the mere absence of legal restraint and makes material and social capacity essential to liberty.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Croly’s Chapter IX argues that reform must respect national traditions and cohesion, with fair notice, public discussion and consent before changing fundamental institutions.

priority-to-poor.rationale: The intellectual history defines the common good to include placing the concerns of the least well-off above narrow self-interest and privileged demands.

promote-democracy-abroad.rationale: Croly’s Chapter X argues that America should help establish an international order enabling democracy abroad and condemns indifference to its spread in Europe.

property-franchise.rationale: The human-rights study presents the UDHR as foundational to progressive values; Articles 2 and 21 in its appendix require political rights without property distinctions and universal equal suffrage.

property-fundamental.rationale: The intellectual history describes progressivism’s rejection of fixed property rights that prevent government from addressing exploitation, suffering and inequality.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: The intellectual history describes progressive property rules as subject to their social consequences and the good of the community rather than immutable individual entitlements.

public-access-to-information.rationale: In Chapter V Dewey makes publicity and the free dissemination of inquiry essential conditions for an informed democratic public.

public-ownership.rationale: Thompson describes progressive proposals for public ownership of natural monopolies alongside rival proposals for regulated private ownership.

racial-franchise.rationale: The human-rights study identifies equal civil rights regardless of race and universal political participation as progressive commitments; its UDHR appendix makes suffrage universal and equal.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Thompson identifies minimum-wage laws among the social-welfare measures progressive writers advocated, particularly for poorly paid women.

reason-over-faith.rationale: The faith study presents religious moral insight alongside secular inquiry as an enduring source of progressive public action rather than treating reason as the exclusive guide.

recall-officials.rationale: Thompson identifies recall as a progressive reform allowing voters to eject elected officials before their term expires.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Thompson identifies extending government regulation over economic activity and curbing corporate power as defining progressive commitments.

restore-past-order.rationale: Compass defines being progressive as deliberately changing unjust existing arrangements rather than preserving an inherited order for its own sake.

restrict-conversion.rationale: The human-rights study’s foundational declaration expressly protects changing religion and manifesting belief in teaching and observance.

results-over-ideology.rationale: The intellectual history identifies judging ideas by their practical consequences, empirical evidence and experimentation as a central progressive value.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: The human-rights study argues for investment in development and essential services for the global poor as a responsibility grounded in universal freedom and security.

right-to-secede.rationale: Croly’s Chapter IV defends the Union’s coercive resistance to Southern secession and argues that national democratic responsibility cannot be displaced by local claims.

self-interest-moral.rationale: The intellectual history identifies the common good and the needs of the least well-off as priorities above narrow self-interest and privileged demands.

separated-powers.rationale: Croly’s Chapter XI argues that dividing executive and legislative responsibility produces ineffective government and proposes concentrating responsibility in accountable elected leadership.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: In Chapters IV and IX Croly identifies the conflict over slavery as the contradiction that made civil war necessary and describes its elimination as the war’s decisive national result.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Shalin describes progressivism’s method as reform and reconstruction of democratic institutions rather than revolutionary replacement of the state.

social-market-economy.rationale: The intellectual history describes a mixed economy in which public regulation and social protection preserve productive activity while checking concentrated private power.

state-as-business.rationale: In Chapter VII Croly argues that a state cannot serve merely as an impartial referee of private competitors: it must deliberately secure the community’s public purposes.

state-harmful.rationale: CAP’s defining account makes active democratic government responsible for regulating business and securing social opportunity; government is an essential instrument of reform.

strong-leader.rationale: Thompson describes progressive proposals to concentrate administrative authority in elected executives so they can carry out public programmes, paired with direct popular accountability.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Croly’s Chapter XII advocates a graduated federal inheritance tax to reduce accumulated inequalities, with rates reaching twenty percent.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Thompson describes progressive income and inheritance taxation as a way to finance social provision and attack the unequal distribution of wealth.

taxation-theft.rationale: Thompson identifies income and inheritance taxes as legitimate progressive means of financing social reform and reducing unequal wealth.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: The intellectual history describes the progressive response as recognising that new technology alone cannot solve persistent human problems and that institutions and social purposes must change.

unions-good.rationale: In Chapter XII Croly calls unions the most effective machinery for improving workers’ economic and social position, while requiring them to serve the public interest.

universal-healthcare.rationale: The human-rights study identifies access to basic health care as an essential progressive social right that government must make effective.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Thompson describes concentrated corporate wealth as a threat to independent citizenship, political democracy and government free from financial domination.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Compass defines progressive change as a collective responsibility requiring active participation and cooperation across civil society and political institutions.

women-suffrage.rationale: Thompson identifies women’s suffrage as a progressive reform required to make government by the people effective.

workplace-democracy.rationale: The intellectual history describes progressive democracy as extending citizens’ control over workplaces as well as government, homes and neighbourhoods.

notes: Later pass checked all statements, including candidates. Read the full CAP intellectual, human-rights and faith studies, Thompson’s scholarly pamphlet, Shalin’s article, Compass’s definition and the complete ThinkProgress article. Downloaded and searched Croly’s seminal book and Dewey’s named political text through the project Gutenberg tool and local corpus, across economy, government, society, world, liberty, culture, ecology, technology, means and globalism. The local reference library contains a Russell review of Dewey’s logic book, not an additional defining progressive political text. Public-office speech and vote corpora cover individual adherents, not the ideology’s own record; party-in-government measures are not treated as official-doctrine regimes. Original Wikipedia sources and the 1912 platform are retained for review history; no current answer rests on Wikipedia or a caucus programme. CAP article pages, Britannica, Oxford, Cambridge, Cairn, Paperity, Sage and Harvard Law Review pages returned HTTP 403; no refused page was retried. The accessible official CAP PDF copies were different copies of the works. GitHub searches found no full-report mirror. Routledge’s full entry is paywalled, so only its visible definition is used. The ThinkProgress article was read as a lead; its handbook excerpts do not license importing further unverified handbook claims. The validator rejected the ThinkProgress definition because its text says progressive rather than naming Progressivism twice; it is therefore not used for answers. Its related claims were checked against qualifying defining sources. Follow-up research concentrated on international affairs, nationalism, local versus central authority, religion, ecology and technology. Croly’s colonial-tutelage prescription is recorded against Compass’s opposed judgment as a split. His hypothetical discussion of an investigation into eugenic restrictions is documented in the nulling rationale rather than excluded as an embarrassing historical excess or converted into a settled policy. Modern sources and the specific canonical texts are distinguished in the rationales. The sources do not provide an ideology-wide position on newer technologies, specific emissions targets, nuclear power, indigenous autonomy or the many other remaining null questions.
